events.text: Two hundred years after the tomb was closed, grave-robbers dig into the mound of the north with iron bars and a lamp. You feel it from your own ridge, far to the south, as a cold place behind the breastbone where the scale used to be. They are in the chamber now. The lamp is up. They are looking at the east wall.

choices.text: Make the painted dragon turn its head

effects.log: The robbers leave their bars, their lamp and one shoe. The story that comes out of the north is that the dragon on the east wall moved, and it frightens every grave-robber in the kingdom for two centuries.

choices.text: Let them look, and let them leave

effects.log: They take the gold and leave the bones. One of them stays behind a long time in front of the east wall with the lamp, not taking anything. Later, much later, that one becomes a painter.

events.text: The capital in your Ward burns a third time. Twice already you have watched the great palace go up in flames, in war and by accident, and twice it was rebuilt. Tonight it is a lamp in the women's quarters and a dry wind, and the whole north wing is alight. Only the banquet pavilion on its stone pillars in the square pond does not burn, and the court is crowding onto it.

choices.text: Rain on the palace, all of it, now

effects.log: A cloudburst out of a clear spring sky. The fire hisses down to smoke. The north wing is lost; nobody is. In the morning the court finds the pond overflowing and a long wet shape pressed into the gravel of the courtyard.

choices.text: Lift the pond over the burning wing

ok.log: The whole pond rises in one sheet and falls on the north wing. The fire is out in a breath. The pavilion stands on its pillars in an empty pond, and the court on it is dripping and amazed.

fail.log: Half the pond falls where you meant it; the other half falls on you. The fire is put out in the end by the court with buckets, and you lie in the empty pond with burnt whiskers. (-15 health)

choices.text: Let it burn. Heaven sends fire to proud houses

effects.log: The north wing burns to the stones. The court weeps on the pavilion until dawn. A palace that burns three times, the people say, is not wanted by heaven, and they say it quietly, looking at your ridge.

events.text: The regent who is rebuilding the palace has a plan against fire, from an old book: cast two dragons of bronze and sink them in the pond under the pavilion, so that water will always sit between the palace and flame. The foundry outside the west gate has poured them already, each as long as a boat, five claws on every foot. The regent stands at the edge of the pond with the rope in one hand and asks the ridge, out loud, for help.

choices.text: Breathe on the bronze before it goes down

effects.log: The two dragons go into the water warm. The regent feels it through the rope and lets go too soon, and they sink side by side, facing the palace, five claws spread. Nothing burns in the capital that year. Or the next.

choices.text: Correct the regent: dragons hold a pearl. These have none

effects.log: The regent looks at the bronze, at the ridge, back at the bronze, and goes very pale. A pearl is cast overnight. The court never knows why the dedication was delayed a day.

choices.text: Laugh. Bronze is not a dragon

effects.log: The two bronze dragons go into the pond anyway. They are very fine, and very still, and you are fairly sure they will do nothing at all.

events.text: A fourth fire, in the sixth year after the rebuilding, and this one is set: a palace plot, oil in the eaves of the throne hall, a rebel prince with torches at three gates. The bronze dragons in the pond are not enough. You can feel them straining at the bottom, two shapes trying to be what they were made to look like.

choices.text: Go down into the pond and become the bronze

effects.log: You go down into the pond under the pavilion and into the cast bronze, between one breath and the next. The pond rises. Every eave in the palace drips. The torches go out at three gates. From then on, as long as the palace stands, no fire takes it, and centuries later, when the pond is dredged, a bronze dragon with five claws and no pearl is found in the mud, and the dredgers swear it was warm.

choices.text: Put out the fire from the sky, and leave the bronze to the bronze

effects.log: A storm on three gates at once. The prince is caught dripping. The throne hall smokes and stands. The bronze dragons lie at the bottom of the pond looking, you think, a little relieved.

choices.text: Let the court see to its own plots

effects.log: The throne hall burns. The regent survives; the prince does not. A dragon who guards a valley, you tell yourself, does not have to guard a palace from its own princes. It sounds less true at night.

events.text: Two hundred years on, the palace still stands and has not burned once. The court has forgotten the bronze dragons in the pond entirely. The pavilion is used for banquets and the examinations, and on hot nights the young scholars dangle their feet in the water and drop their brushes in it and do not know what is underneath.

choices.text: Visit the bronze dragons one night

effects.log: You go down into the pond in the dark. The bronze is green now, and one of them has lost a claw to a careless anchor. You lie between them till dawn. They are very good company, for bronze.

choices.text: Return a scholar's brush, very wet

effects.log: The brush comes up out of the pond and lands on the scholar's desk. The scholar passes the examination the next week with the best essay in a decade, and spends the rest of a long career refusing to explain the brush.

events.text: There is a deep pond under the north end of your ridge where you have let lesser dragons live for centuries: eight of them, river dragons and pond dragons, small, quarrelsome, fond of hailstorms. A great monk has come to the pond: {npc}, back from the west with relics of the Buddha in a box, who wants exactly this ground for a temple. For a hundred days {npc} sits at the water's edge and chants, and prays, and copies sutras, asking the dragons to leave.

choices.text: Rise and speak with {him} as one guardian to another

effects.log: {npc} listens with complete attention, palms together. "I do not want to drive anyone out," {he} says. "But the relics must rest on this ground, and nowhere else. I have looked for nine years." You believe {him}. That is the trouble.

choices.text: Tell the eight to leave. A temple is not the worst neighbour

effects.log: The eight do not listen to you any more than they listen to {npc}. They are small dragons, and stubborn, and the pond is theirs. They send hail on the monk's straw hut every night for a month.

choices.text: Let the monk sit. The pond is yours

effects.log: The chanting goes on for the hundred days. {npc} never once looks at your ridge, and on the hundred-and-first morning, {he} gets up, and goes to find paper and ink.

events.text: {npc} writes one character on a sheet of paper: fire. Throws it into the air over the pond. Stirs the water with a long staff, once, sunwise. The pond begins to steam, then to simmer, then to boil, and the eight lesser dragons come up out of it screaming. Three of them, blind with steam, fly straight into the hillside, and the rock there turns red. Five go south down the valley and do not stop. You are in the pond too.

choices.text: Pull the three from the hillside and carry them to the river

effects.log: Two of them live. The rock where they hit stays red; the valley will call it Dragon Blood Rock for a thousand years. You come back for the pond with your scales half-scalded. (-20 health)

choices.text: Rise against {npc}: turn the monk's own steam back on {him}

ok.log: The staff breaks. {npc} is thrown into the pines and gets up very slowly, and looks at you with sorrow rather than anger, which is worse. The pond keeps boiling. A word, once written, is hard to take back.

fail.log: You cannot reach {npc}. The character for fire hangs in the air between you, written in a hand steadier than yours. (-25 health)

choices.text: Stay in the boiling pond

effects.log: The water is fire. You stay. You are not sure, yourself, whether it is stubbornness or something better. The monk on the bank stops stirring and watches you with great attention. (-15 health)

events.text: The pond stops boiling. You are still in it. The world has gone white: the steam took your eyes. {npc} kneels on the bank and speaks to you very gently. "Everyone else is gone. You stayed. Tell me why, and tell me what you want, and if it can be given I will give it."

choices.text: "Let me stay, blind, and I will guard your temple for ever"

effects.log: {npc} agrees with tears running down. The temple is built around the pond; the relics rest beside it; the great hall has no image in it, only a window looking onto the relics, and the pond. You live there blind for the rest of your long life, listening to the bells, and no fire, no war, no thief ever takes that temple, and the monks still put food on the water for you at dawn.

choices.text: "Give me back the pond for one year to heal, and I will go"

effects.log: A year in the pond, with the monk bringing medicinal roots to the bank every morning. At the end of it your sight comes back, clouded, a little, and you go back to the ridge and give the ground to the relics. The temple is built. You visit it on the equinoxes.

choices.text: "Nothing from you"

effects.log: You leave the pond blind and feel your way along your own ridge by the pines. It takes ten years for your eyes to clear. The temple is built without your blessing, and prospers anyway, which you find hard to forgive.

events.text: The temple at the north end of your ridge has grown into one of the great temples of the land. Pilgrims come from every province to see the relics. Very few of them notice the small dark pond beside the great hall, or the custom, older than anyone can explain, of putting a bowl of rice on its water at dawn.

choices.text: Visit the pond on the spring equinox

effects.log: An old monk sweeping the steps sees a ripple in the pond that is far too big, and puts down the broom, and bows to it. Some things are remembered in the body after the reason is gone.

choices.text: Send the two dragons who lived to live there

effects.log: Two small hail-loving dragons move into the temple pond. They send hail onto the roof of the abbot's quarters every winter, which the monks decide to regard as a teaching.

events.text: A great gut on the hill above the valley at the start of spring: a mudang in layered robes of the five colours, two drummers, a cymbal player, and five long flags on bamboo poles, blue, red, white, black and yellow. The mudang dances to each direction in turn and calls its emperor down: Bukbang Heukje of the north, Nambang Jeokje of the south, Seobang Baekje of the west, Jungang Hwangje of the centre. Then she turns east, raises the blue flag, and calls on the Blue Emperor of the East. She means you.

choices.text: Come down into the blue flag

effects.log: The blue silk fills like a sail on a windless morning and the mudang staggers, laughing, and the drummers lose the beat. Every plum tree on the hillside opens at once. The village will talk about nothing else until the harvest.

choices.text: Come as the green wind only, and let the rite go on

effects.log: A warm east wind runs once round the hill and through the blue flag and away. The mudang feels it and finishes the rite as if nothing happened, which is how the best of them do it.

choices.text: You are a dragon, not an emperor. Stay on the ridge

effects.log: The mudang calls three times and then, smiling, moves on to the next part of the rite. The blue flag hangs still. Spring comes anyway, a week late, and nobody minds.

events.text: After the rite, the mudang lets the village pick a fortune from the five flags, rolled tight on their poles: pull one blindly, and the colour tells the year. One small child from the first house, {npc}, has pulled the blue flag five years running, and the mudang has started to look at the ridge thoughtfully while {he} does it.

choices.text: Let {him} pull blue again

mem.note: gave me the blue flag every year

effects.log: Six years. Then seven. When {npc} is grown, the mudang takes the child of the blue flag as an apprentice, and the valley has a mudang of its own who never once has to call the east twice.

choices.text: Let {him} pull red this year, so the world does not seem arranged for one child

effects.log: Red: a hot year, a hard one. {npc} cries, then works harder than anyone in the valley all summer, and pulls blue again the next spring, and is much less surprised about it.

events.text: You notice, one spring, that you cannot find the edge of yourself. The green wind going over the paddies is you. The sap rising in the pines is you. The first shoots of bracken on the north slope, the cuckoo, the softening of the river ice: you, all of it, everywhere at once. On the far side of the year the black tortoise of the north is holding winter out to you, like a cup handed across a table, and waiting for you to take it.

choices.text: Take the cup

effects.log: Winter goes into you and comes out spring. It is not a thing you do. It is a thing that happens through you, as water happens through a valley. The Black Tortoise nods both heads and goes back north to wait for autumn.

choices.text: Pull yourself back into one body, for now

effects.log: You gather up the wind, the sap, the cuckoo, all of it, back into a long blue-green body on a ridge. It feels small. It feels like home. Spring that year is a little late, and very local.

events.text: The Jade court sends for you. Far beyond the four directions there is a world where spring has not come for three hundred years: frozen rivers, seeds asleep in the ground, a people who have forgotten what blossom looks like and paint it from old books. "The Blue Emperor of the East," says the envoy, "is asked to carry spring there. It is a long way. You may not come back the same."

choices.text: Go, and carry spring

effects.log: It takes a century. River by river, field by field, you breathe on a frozen world until the ice goes grey and then black and then, one morning, a child there sees a green shoot and does not know the word for it. You come home thinner, and lighter, and somehow larger.

choices.text: Send the green wind, and stay with your own valley

effects.log: The wind goes alone across the dark between worlds. It arrives tired. Spring there, when it comes, is thin and pale, but it comes, and that is more than they had.

choices.text: Ask why heaven let it freeze

effects.log: The envoy does not answer for a long time. "Because nobody went," it says at last. "That is usually why." You do not go either, that century. You think about it in every spring after.

events.text: The spring rite on the hill, as every year for centuries. The mudang is the great-great-granddaughter of the mudang who first called you down, or someone very like her. She turns east, lifts the blue flag, and calls the Blue Emperor of the East. And this time, you feel it all the way through: if you answer, you will answer as spring, and not come back as a dragon. The flag waits. The drums wait. Every seed in the valley waits.

choices.text: Answer as spring

effects.log: You let go of the ridge, the scales, the long blue-green body, the name, and go out into the year. The blue flag fills. Every plum tree in the land opens at once. There is no dragon on the ridge any more. There is only spring, every spring, for ever, and it is your breath, and the mudang on the hill, weeping and laughing, is the first to feel it.

choices.text: Answer as a dragon, one more time

effects.log: You come down into the blue flag as you did long ago, a dragon, and the mudang staggers under the weight and laughs, and the village sees you whole. There will be another spring for the other answer. You are fairly sure.

choices.text: Let her call, and stay still, and listen

effects.log: She calls three times. You listen to all three. You think it is the most beautiful thing you have ever heard, a human voice calling spring by its name. Spring comes anyway, from somewhere inside you, without your having to decide.

events.text: Spring on the hill, the drums, the five flags, the mudang turning east. Another year of the rite. The faces in the crowd change every generation; the rite does not. A grandmother holds a baby up toward the blue flag so the Blue Emperor can see it, and the baby sneezes.

choices.text: Bless the baby

effects.log: A warm gust, smelling of plum blossom, ruffles the baby's hair. It sneezes again. The grandmother is satisfied. That child will never once, in a long life, have a bad spring.

choices.text: Bless the whole hill

effects.log: Every bush on the hill flowers at once, and the drummers lose the beat, and the mudang, who has seen this before, simply waits, smiling, until they find it again.

events.text: The first full moon of the year. You are older than any tree in the valley, and you find yourself at the old well in the valley at first cockcrow without having meant to come: a stone ring, a wooden lid, a gourd ladle on a string. Down there, on the cold stones under the water, you were an egg. The women are coming up the lanes in the dark with water jars, racing, as they always have, to be first.

choices.text: Watch the race from the willow

effects.log: A young woman wins by a step, draws the first water, and floats a straw on what is left in the well, so the others will know. She has no idea there is a dragon in the willow, crying a little, for no reason it can name.

choices.text: Lay a blessing on the first water

effects.log: Whoever wins carries a year of good harvest home in a jar. She does not know it is from you. Nobody ever does. That was always the point.

events.text: A grey clerk of heaven sits on the rim of the old well on the first full moon, swinging its feet, a ledger in its lap. "Some go to the sky," it says. "Some go into the ridge, or the sea, or a wall. And a few, a very few, ask to go back to the beginning, an egg in a well, and do it all again remembering everything. It is allowed. It is not encouraged. I thought you might like to know."

choices.text: Ask why anyone would choose it

effects.log: "To get it right," says the clerk. "Or to get it wrong differently. Or because they liked the first year, in the water jar, better than all the rest." It shrugs. "Dragons are sentimental. It is in the file."

choices.text: Ask whether you would remember the people

effects.log: "All of them," says the clerk. "That is the cost. They will not remember you." It closes the ledger. "Think about it. You have time. You have, if anything, too much."

events.text: Another first full moon. The clerk is back on the well rim, and does not open the ledger. Behind you on the ridge the whole valley you kept is asleep; above you the Eastern Palace is lit. "Well?" says the clerk. Down in the black water, on the cold stones, there is a space exactly the size of a fist, waiting.

choices.text: Go back down into the well

effects.log: You get smaller and smaller and go down into the water as a drop goes, and then there are cold stones, and a full moon very far above, and a blue-green shell around you, and the first cock crows. Somewhere a woman is running up a lane with a jar. You remember everything. This time you will know her name.

choices.text: Stay. This life is not finished

effects.log: The clerk nods as if it expected nothing else and is gone before the cock crows. A woman runs up the lane with a jar, draws the first water, floats her straw, and goes home with a good year. You walk back to the ridge in the frost.

choices.text: Ask the clerk to keep the place for you, for later

effects.log: "For later," the clerk repeats, and writes it in the ledger in very small characters. "We will see. Wells are patient, but not that patient." It does not say no.
